newsitem.title: NICARAGUA: Costa Rican president hospitalized, then released.
newsitem.headline: Costa Rican president hospitalized, then released.

text.p: Costa Rican President Jose Maria Figueres collapsed with chest pains during a ceremony in Nicaragua on Monday and was rushed to a hospital though later released, witnesses and officials said.

After being kept under observation for two hours, Figueres was released and rejoined the other Central American presidents at a ceremony paying tribute to Nicaraguan President Violeta Chamorro, army hospital spokesman Rolando Brenes told Reuters.
"The doctors have determined that he suffered a digestive disorder, that his condition is satisfactory, and that he can resume his functions," Brenes said.
Initial reports on state-owned Radio Nicaragua said Figueres, 42, had suffered a heart attack.

Witnesses said Figueres was standing outdoors in Managua's Plaza of the Republic as Chamorro addressed a group of Nicaraguan children when he collapsed on his chair and was rushed in an ambulance to the local hospital.
A statement from the Costa Rican government said Figueres suffered from "dyspepsia, characterised by tightness of the chest," for which Figueres was hospitalized for "routine tests."

"I have spoken on the telephone and been informed that he (Figueres) is going over the final touches to a speech he will give later tonight," presidential spokesman Alejandro Soto told reporters in San Jose, the capital of Costa Rica.
Figueres and the heads of state from Honduras, El Salvador, Guatemala, Panama and Belize were in Managua paying tribute to Chamorro, who leaves office on Jan. 10.

This is the second time Figueres has been hospitalized while in office. In 1995, Figueres's small government plane skidded off a runway in rural Costa Rica. He was hospitalized for a week for injuries to his legs, chest and neck and wore a surgical collar for a few days after being released.

Figueres is the son of Jose "Pepe" Figueres, considered the father of Central American democracy, who abolished the Costa Rican army 48 years ago in a move widely seen as responsible for the relative prosperity of that country in a highly impoverished region.
